subtype: Stamping and slamming out in anger [Regulating]
passage:
"No cricket until the project's done, Mridul. That's final."
"But everyone's going! You never—"
"I heard you. The answer's still no," said his stepdad, Francis.
"This is SO unfair!" Stamp, stamp, stamp down the corridor. BANG went the bedroom door.

Later: knock, knock. "Can I come in?"
"…Fine."
"You were really angry. It's okay to need to leave. Slamming the door, not so okay."
"You didn't even listen."
"Then let's make a deal. Next time, say 'I need a walk,' go round the building, and when you come back we talk properly. I'll listen then. Deal?"
"…Can it be round the building twice?"
"Twice is fine."

qa.q: What was Mridul not allowed to go to until the project was done?
qa.a: Cricket.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he stamped down the corridor?
qa.a: Furious and unheard, sure the rule was unfair, and needing to get away from the argument.

qa.q: What cooling-off routine did they agree on?
qa.a: Mridul says "I need a walk", goes round the building (twice is fine), and then comes back to talk while Francis listens.

qa.q: How might Francis feel hearing the door bang?
qa.a: He is probably annoyed at the slam but can also see how angry Mridul is, which is why he comes to talk instead of shouting back.

grounding: It shows a child stamping off and slamming a door after losing an argument, and an adult turning the urge to leave into a walk-then-talk routine.

passage:
"Santosh, why are you all wrapped up like a samosa?"
"I'm not."
"You've got both arms round yourself and Bhalu squashed under your chin."
"…The ghost part's coming."
Akash bhaiya paused the film. "Cold, or scared?"
"Bit of both. The fan's on full."
"Want me to switch the film off?"
"No! I want to see how it ends."
"Okay. Fan down, shawl on, and I'll sit right here. If it gets too much, we stop. No teasing."
"Promise no teasing?"
"Promise."
Santosh loosened one arm, just enough to hold the edge of the shawl.

qa.q: What was Santosh holding under his chin?
qa.a: Bhalu, squashed under his chin.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling as he hugged himself and Bhalu?
qa.a: A bit scared of the coming ghost part and a bit cold from the fan, as he admits; the hug was his way of soothing himself.

qa.q: What made Akash bhaiya's check-in work?
qa.a: He asked a quiet question, "Cold, or scared?", instead of assuming or teasing, then fixed the cold and stayed close 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Akash bhaiya had laughed at the "samosa" and kept the film going?
qa.a: Santosh might hide the fear, feel ashamed and scared alone, and be less likely to say what he needs next time.

grounding: It shows a child hugging himself and a soft toy during a scary film, and an older brother checking in quietly instead of assuming.

passage:
Rain hammered the roof of the school bus, and the attendant was up front arguing with the driver about the wipers. At the back, two Class 7 boys leaned over Reena's seat. "Oi, specky! Show us your frog eyes." One flicked her glasses.

Reena ducked, pulled her hood down and covered her face with both arms.

Sabina's friend giggled. "She's such a baby."

Sabina didn't laugh. That wasn't babyish; Reena was shaking. "Stop it," Sabina said loudly, and slid in beside Reena. At the school gate she took Reena straight to Mrs Pinto on duty and told her everything. Mrs Pinto listened, thanked them both and sent for the two boys before first period.

qa.q: What did one of the boys flick?
qa.a: Reena's glasses.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling as she ducked and covered her face?
qa.a: Frightened and hurt by the taunts, not babyish; her shaking shows how scared she was.

qa.q: Which choices did Sabina make that helped Reena?
qa.a: She refused to laugh, told the boys to stop, sat beside Reena and took her straight to Mrs Pinto, a teacher.

qa.q: How did Sabina's friend read Reena's ducking?
qa.a: The friend saw it as babyish and giggled, missing that Reena was frightened and in pain.

grounding: It shows a child recognising a peer's ducking and face-covering during a taunt as fear, stopping, helping and telling a teacher.

subtype: Scratching the head and forehead rubbing [Interpreting]
passage:
"Mahima, you've scratched your head about fifty times," Shreya whispered across their shared desk.
"Have I?"
"And now you're rubbing your forehead. Stuck on the worksheet?"
"Not stuck. Itchy! Amma oiled my hair last night, and now my whole head's crawling."
"Eww. Okay."
"And I slept really late because of my cousin's wedding. My brain feels like cotton."
"So not confused, just itchy and tired?"
Mahima looked at the page again. "Well… number six is a bit confusing."
"Want to do it together?"
"Yes, please. But don't lean on my oily head."

qa.q: What had Amma done the night before?
qa.a: Amma oiled Mahima's hair last night.

qa.q: Why did Mahima keep scratching and rubbing her forehead?
qa.a: Mostly because her oiled head itched and she felt tired after a late night; only a little because she felt confused by number six.

qa.q: What did Shreya do that worked better than guessing?
qa.a: She asked a friendly "Stuck on the worksheet?", which uncovered the real reasons and still led to help with number six.

qa.q: What would change if Shreya had told the teacher that Mahima didn't understand anything?
qa.a: Mahima would feel embarrassed and misjudged, since the scratching was mostly itching and tiredness.

grounding: It shows a child seeing a partner scratch her head and rub her forehead, and a friendly are-you-stuck question revealing an itch and tiredness.

passage:
"Your turn, Zubin. Tell us about your trip to Ladakh."
"Um. Okay." Zubin tugged his sleeve down over his wrist. "We saw a lake that was three different blues."
He straightened his collar. Then his tie. Then his collar again.
"He's making it up," muttered Karan. "Look at him fiddling."
"He's not," Rafiq whispered back. "He does that every time he has to talk in front of people. He did it at his own birthday."
"…And a yak walked right past our tent." Zubin tugged the other sleeve.
Karan snorted. "A yak?"
"There are yaks in Ladakh, Karan," said Ms Iyer. "Go on, Zubin. Did it notice you?"
Zubin's hands dropped to his sides. "It sniffed my shoe."

qa.q: What did Zubin say the lake looked like?
qa.a: A lake that was three different blues.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling as he tugged his sleeves and kept straightening his collar?
qa.a: Nervous and self-conscious about speaking in front of the class; the tugging comforted him and says nothing about whether his story is true.

qa.q: How did Ms Iyer help Zubin relax?
qa.a: She backed up his fact about yaks and asked a friendly question, so his hands dropped to his sides.

qa.q: How did Rafiq see the fiddling, compared with Karan?
qa.a: Rafiq knew it was Zubin's usual nervous habit, while Karan wrongly took it as a sign of making things up.

grounding: It shows a child tugging sleeves and straightening his collar from nerves while speaking, which a classmate wrongly reads as lying.

passage:
Monday: Jasleen and Navpreet walked to school hand in hand, swinging their arms like always. Her cousin Hrithik, visiting from Toronto, smirked. "Are you two a couple?" Jasleen rolled her eyes. "She's my best friend. Here lots of friends do this."

Wednesday: After Jasleen's shaky dance at assembly, Mrs Gill patted her twice on the back. "Brave effort." Jasleen's shoulders relaxed. A pat from Ma'am meant well done.

Friday: At tuition, a boy grabbed her wrist to drag her into tag and wouldn't let go. It didn't feel like a friend's hand. "Let go. I don't like that," she said, and pulled free. She told the tuition teacher straight away. The teacher spoke to the boy right then and told Jasleen she was right to say no and to tell.

qa.q: Where was Hrithik visiting from?
qa.a: From Toronto.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling on Friday when the boy wouldn't let go of her wrist?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and uneasy, because it didn't feel like a friend's hand; she was firm enough to say no and pull free.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do on Friday that was wise?
qa.a: She said clearly, "Let go. I don't like that," pulled free and told the tuition teacher straight away.

qa.q: How did Hrithik read the hand-holding on Monday?
qa.a: Hrithik read it as romance, perhaps because friends there hold hands less often; for Jasleen it simply meant friendship.

grounding: It shows a child reading hand-holding and a teacher's pat as friendship and reassurance, and refusing and reporting a touch that felt wrong.

passage:
Saturday

WE WON the inter-school quiz! 🎉 When they called our name, I high-fived Aman so hard my palm stung. Then the chief guest shook all our hands, very serious, like we were grown-ups.

I held out my hand to Noor for a high-five too, but she just smiled and waved. I felt a bit silly with my hand hanging there. On the bus I asked if she was cross with me. She said no, she just doesn't like touching much, even with friends, and waving is how she does it. So we made up a secret wave: two wiggly fingers and a salute. Aman wants a fist-bump version.

Vijay

qa.q: What did the chief guest do?
qa.a: The chief guest shook all their hands, very seriously.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel with a hand hanging in the air?
qa.a: A bit silly and unsure, wondering whether Noor was cross.

qa.q: What did Vijay do that fixed the awkward moment?
qa.a: Vijay asked Noor on the bus instead of assuming, and then they made up a secret wave together.

qa.q: How does Noor prefer to celebrate with friends, and why?
qa.a: Noor prefers a wave because she doesn't like touching much, even with friends; it has nothing to do with being cross.

grounding: It is a child's diary about high-fives, handshakes and fist bumps as warm quick touches, and a friend who prefers a wave instead.

passage:
In their Stockholm classroom, Emeka and Oskar had been building the volcano together for a week. Then Emeka called Oskar's lava idea "dumb". Oskar went red, picked up his paints and moved to the table by the window, his back turned.

Emeka stared at that back all afternoon. At pickup he wanted to run after him and say, "Just talk to me!" His older sister shook her head. "Maybe he needs space. Try something small."

That night Emeka wrote on a card: "Sorry I said dumb. Your lava idea was good. Paint it together tomorrow?" He slid it into Oskar's cubby in the morning. By break, Oskar's paints were back on their table.

qa.q: Where did Oskar move to?
qa.a: The table by the window.

qa.q: What was Oskar most likely feeling when he moved away and turned his back?
qa.a: Hurt and angry that his idea was called dumb; he may also simply have needed space to calm down.

qa.q: Why did the card work better than chasing Oskar at pickup?
qa.a: It gave Oskar space, apologised clearly and made a friendly invitation, instead of pushing him to talk before he was ready.

qa.q: How did Emeka's sister see the situation?
qa.a: She saw that Oskar might need space and that pushing could make it worse, so she suggested something small.

grounding: It shows a child noticing a friend move tables and turn away after an argument, and a kind note later repairing more than pushing.

subtype: Leaning closer to share and secrets [Expressing]
passage:
At break in a Berlin schoolyard, Ines leaned in close to Selin, cupping her hand round Selin's ear. "My cat had kittens last night. Five!"

Selin squealed, and Ines pulled out her phone. Their heads almost touched as they bent over the tiny screen.

Behind them, Johanna, who had only joined the class that week, hovered with her lunchbox, looking at the ground. Selin noticed first and nudged Ines. Ines hesitated. The kittens were a bit of a secret. Then she tilted the phone. "Johanna, want to see? They're so small their eyes aren't open."

Johanna stepped in, and three heads bent over the screen.

qa.q: How many kittens did Ines's cat have?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: Why did Ines hesitate before tilting the phone?
qa.a: She felt a little protective of her news, since the kittens were a bit of a secret shared with Selin; she was torn between keeping it close and including Johanna.

qa.q: What small choice made Johanna feel included?
qa.a: Ines tilted the phone and invited Johanna by name to see the kittens.

qa.q: How might Johanna feel watching the two heads almost touching?
qa.a: As a newcomer she likely felt left out and lonely, which is why she hovered and looked at the ground.

grounding: It shows children leaning in close to whisper and share a phone screen as a sign of trust, and including a left-out newcomer.

passage:
At skit practice in the school activity room in Chennai, Rekha tripped over her own dupatta and landed on a beanbag. She lay there giggling. "Graceful swan, that's me!" Everyone laughed, Rekha loudest.

Ten minutes later it was Shreya's line. "Mother, pass me the re-sipe book."

Someone snorted. Nitin copied her in a squeaky voice, "re-SIPE", and a few others laughed. Shreya didn't. Her ears went red, and she stared at her script.

Rekha felt the difference like a draught of cold air. The first laugh had been hers to share; this one was being done to Shreya. "It's a weird word," Rekha said. "I said it that way till Class 5. Go on, Shreya."

qa.q: What did Rekha trip over?
qa.a: Her own dupatta.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when her ears went red and she stared at her script?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt, because the others were laughing at her mistake, not with her.

qa.q: What did Rekha do to stop the mocking laughter?
qa.a: She didn't join in; she said it's a weird word, admitted she said it the same way till Class 5, and told Shreya to go on.

qa.q: How might Nitin see his squeaky copy?
qa.a: Nitin may think it was harmless fun, like the laugh at Rekha's fall, without noticing that Shreya wasn't laughing.

grounding: It shows a child telling shared laughter at her own fall from laughter that mocks a classmate's mistake, and refusing to join in.
